name: OD260 to Nucleic Acid Concentration Calculator
seoTitle: OD260 to Nucleic Acid Concentration Calculator
seoDesc: A260 converts to concentration with a factor that depends on what you are measuring: 50 for double-stranded DNA, 40 for RNA, 33 for single-stranded DNA. Free
h1: OD260 to Nucleic Acid Concentration Calculator
summary:
A260 converts to concentration with a factor that depends on what you are measuring: 50 for double-stranded DNA, 40 for RNA, 33 for single-stranded DNA. It returns concentration, A260/A280 and total yield in 100 µL, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator applies the right factor, the dilution, and the A260/A280 ratio that tells you whether the sample is clean. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the OD260 to Nucleic Acid Concentration
sections.html:
Concentration (ng/µL) = A260 × dilution × factor, with factor 50 (dsDNA), 40 (RNA), 33 (ssDNA)

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
A260absorbance at 260 nmAU
factor50 ng/µL per A260 for dsDNAng/µL
purityA260/A280ratio

Where the relationship comes from. Factors of 50, 40 and 33 ng/µL per A260 unit are the standard convention for dsDNA, RNA and ssDNA.

sections.title: How do I use the OD260 to Nucleic Acid Concentration?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: nucleic acid set to 50.0, a260 reading of 0.42, dilution factor of 1 ×, a280 reading of 0.23.

Substituting them into the formula gives concentration of 21,000 ng/µL, a260/a280 of 1.83, total yield in 100 µl of 2,100 µg.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
1.8Pure DNAthe usual target for dsDNA
2.0Pure RNAthe usual target for RNA
below 1.6Protein or phenol carry-overre-purify before sequencing

  • The factors assume a 1 cm path length. A Nanodrop normalises to 1 cm automatically; a microplate reader does not, so check the path length.

  • A260 measures everything that absorbs at 260 nm, including free nucleotides and primers, so a high concentration with a poor 260/280 can still fail downstream.

  • Below about 0.1 AU the reading is dominated by noise; use a fluorescent assay instead.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Using the dsDNA factor for RNA (50 instead of 40, a 25% overestimate).
  • Forgetting the dilution when the sample was diluted for the reading.
  • Reading a sample that still has ethanol in it — ethanol absorbs strongly in the UV.

faq.a: A 50 µg/mL solution of double-stranded DNA in a 1 cm cuvette has an A260 of 1.0.

faq.q: My A260/A280 is 1.9 but the sequencing failed — why?
faq.a: The ratio is insensitive to some inhibitors; check A260/A230 and run a gel.

faq.q: What does the OD260 to Nucleic Acid Concentration actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns concentration, A260/A280 and total yield in 100 µL. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
